title: From Copilot to Colleague: Trustworthy Agents for High-Stakes - Joel Hron, CTO Thomson Reuters

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The keynote centers on architecting agentic AI systems for high-stakes professional domains, presenting a four-dial framework for agent design and demonstrating legacy system decomposition into agent tools for tax and legal research workflows.

summary: Joel Hron, CTO of Thomson Reuters, frames the keynote around a north star shift from AI being merely helpful to being productive—producing outputs, making judgments, and taking decisions on behalf of users in high-stakes domains like law, tax, global trade, risk, and fraud investigations. Thomson Reuters brings over 100 years of domain expertise, 4,500 domain experts, 1.5+ TB of proprietary content, a 200+ scientist applied research lab, and $200M+ annual AI investment. Hron cites Y Combinator's directive to build law firms of agents rather than agentic tools for law firms, underscoring the profound shift. He defines agentic AI not as binary but as a spectrum with four dials: autonomy, context, memory, and coordination, each tunable per use case and risk tolerance. Lessons learned include: evals are the hardest challenge because users expect determinism from non-deterministic systems, and domain experts show 10%+ accuracy swings on identical questions a week apart; legacy applications are assets when decomposed into agent tools; the MVP mindset proved counterproductive—only by building the whole system could teams see what components mattered. Two demos illustrate these lessons. The tax demo shows end-to-end return generation from source documents through data extraction, field mapping, rule application, validation, and filing, leveraging a built-in validation engine that lets the AI inspect errors and seek more document information. The legal research demo shows an AI assistant using litigation research product components as tools—searching, fetching, comparing and validating citations across case law, statutes, regulations, and licensed content—writing notes along its trajectory and producing a final report with hard citations to true cases and statutes, flagging associated risks. Hron wraps up with strategic advice: begin with the whole problem in mind, treat agency as a lever not a binary, bring life to old systems by decomposing them into agent tools, focus on human-in-the-loop evaluation, and identify unique assets for differentiation. In Q&A, he addresses cybersecurity posture for government and financial firms, noting FedRAMP compliance and adaptation to evolving standards like the recent ISO standard.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The north star for AI assistants has shifted from helpfulness to productive—systems must produce output and make decisions, not just suggest.
Agentic AI is a spectrum, not a binary; four dials (autonomy, context, memory, coordination) are tuned per use case and risk tolerance.
Evals are the hardest problem: users expect determinism, domain experts show 10%+ swings on repeated judgments, and agentic drift amplifies difficulty.
Legacy applications with highly tuned domain logic are unique assets when decomposed into agent tools, not baggage to discard.
The MVP mindset caused teams to overindex on minimal; building the whole system first revealed which components mattered and what the agentic nature healed.
Identify your organization's unique assets (domain experts, proprietary content) and leverage them for differentiation—Thomson Reuters' 4,500 experts and 1.5+ TB of content are theirs.
Legal research agents can write notes to themselves along their trajectory, rationalizing findings into a final report with hard citations and risk flags.
Security and compliance (FedRAMP, ISO standards) are evolving quickly; adaptability is essential for government and financial sector deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and Thomson Reuters Context
sections.summary: Hron introduces the shift from helpful to productive AI assistants in high-stakes domains. He provides Thomson Reuters context: 100+ year company, 97% of top 100 US law firms, 99% of Fortune 100, 4,500 domain experts, 1.5+ TB proprietary content, $3B+ in acquisitions, 200+ scientists, $200M+/year on AI development.

sections.title: Agentic AI as a Spectrum
sections.summary: Hron cites Y Combinator's directive to build law firms of agents. He defines agentic AI as a spectrum with four tunable dials: autonomy (discrete task to self-evolving workflow), context (parametric to multi-source to schema mutation), memory (stateless to persistent cross-session), and coordination (atomic execution to multi-agent collaboration).

sections.title: Lessons Learned: Evals, Legacy Apps, and MVPs
sections.summary: Hron shares three lessons: evals are hardest due to non-determinism, expert variability (10%+ swings), and agentic drift; legacy applications are assets when decomposed into agent tools; the MVP mindset caused teams to overindex on minimal, and building the whole system first was the necessary mindset shift.

sections.title: Demo: End-to-End Tax Return Generation
sections.summary: Hron demos a tax use case where AI takes source documents (W2, 1099), extracts data, maps to tax engine fields, applies tax law rules, and validates work via a built-in validation engine that inspects errors and seeks more document information to resolve and finish the workflow, illustrating legacy system decomposition.

sections.title: Demo: Legal Research with Citation Linking
sections.summary: Hron demos a legal research use case where an AI assistant uses litigation research product components as tools—searching, fetching, comparing and validating citations across case law, statutes, regulations, and licensed content. The agent writes notes along its trajectory and produces a final report with hard citations to true cases/statutes and risk flags.

sections.title: Wrap-Up: Strategic Advice and Unique Assets
sections.summary: Hron wraps up with strategic guidance: begin with the whole problem in mind, treat agency as a dial not a binary, bring life to old systems by decomposing them into agent tools, focus on human-in-the-loop evaluation, and identify unique organizational assets (like Thomson Reuters' 4,500 experts and terabytes of content) for differentiation.

sections.title: Q&A: Cybersecurity Posture for Government and Financial Sectors
sections.summary: A DoD-sponsored PhD student asks about cybersecurity posture including LLM firewalls, guardrails, and vulnerability scanning. Hron notes Thomson Reuters' focus on FedRAMP compliance and conformance to emerging standards like the recent ISO standard, acknowledging the space is evolving quickly and the company is adaptable.

demonstrations: Tax use case demo: AI takes source documents (W2, 1099), extracts data, maps to tax engine fields, applies tax laws, validates work via built-in validation engine, inspects errors, seeks more document information, and generates a tax return end-to-end.

Legal research demo: AI assistant uses litigation research product components as tools (searching, fetching, comparing citations, validating citations) across case law, statutes, regulations, and licensed content, writes notes along its trajectory, and produces a final report with hard citations to true cases/statutes and risk flags.
